title: Telling your own story
goal: Put together a complete story about yourself — past, present and plans — using everything in this book at once.
bekal: link sentences into a flowing paragraph, not a list
move between three tenses within one story

dialogs.title: حِوَار — فِي حَفْلِ الْوَدَاعِ
dialogs.intro: Budi's last evening in Cairo. A guest asks him to tell his story.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: بِكُلِّ سُرُورٍ. اِسْمِي بُودِي، وَأَنَا مِنْ جَاكَرْتَا.
lines.baca: bikulli suruur. ismii Buudii, wa anaa min Jaakartaa.
lines.id: With pleasure. My name is Budi, and I'm from Jakarta.
lines.literal: with all pleasure. name-my Budi, and I from Jakarta.

lines.speaker: ضَيْف:
lines.text: وَمَاذَا كُنْتَ تَعْمَلُ قَبْلَ أَنْ تَأْتِيَ؟
lines.baca: wa maadhaa kunta ta'malu qabla an ta'tiya?
lines.id: And what did you do before you came here?
lines.literal: and what were-you you-work before that you-come?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: كُنْتُ مُهَنْدِسًا فِي شَرِكَةٍ صَغِيرَةٍ لِمُدَّةِ خَمْسِ سَنَوَاتٍ.
lines.baca: kuntu muhandisan fii sharikatin ṣaghiiratin limuddati khamsi sanawaat.
lines.id: I was an engineer at a small company for five years.
lines.literal: was-I engineer in company small for five years.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: لِأَنِّي كُنْتُ أَقْرَأُ الْحُرُوفَ وَلَا أَفْهَمُ شَيْئًا. أَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَفْهَمَ.
lines.baca: li'annii kuntu aqra'ul-huruufa wa laa afhamu shai'an. aradtu an afhama.
lines.id: Because I could read the letters but didn't understand a thing. I wanted to understand.
lines.literal: because-I was-I I-read the-letters and not I-understand something. I-wanted that I-understand.

lines.speaker: ضَيْف:
lines.text: جَوَابٌ جَمِيلٌ. وَكَيْفَ كَانَتِ السَّنَةُ هُنَا؟
lines.baca: jawaabun jamiil. wa kaifa kaanatis-sanatu hunaa?
lines.id: A beautiful answer. And how was the year here?
lines.literal: answer beautiful. and how was the-year here?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: صَعْبَةً فِي الْبِدَايَةِ، ثُمَّ أَصْبَحَتْ أَجْمَلَ سَنَةٍ فِي حَيَاتِي.
lines.baca: ṣa'batan fil-bidaayah, thumma aṣbahat ajmala sanatin fii hayaatii.
lines.id: Hard at first, then it became the best year of my life.
lines.literal: hard in the-beginning, then it-became most-beautiful year in life-my.

lines.speaker: ضَيْف:
lines.id: What was the hardest thing you faced?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: أَنْ أَتَكَلَّمَ بِدُونِ خَوْفٍ. اَلْقَوَاعِدُ أَسْهَلُ مِنَ الشَّجَاعَةِ.
lines.baca: an atakallama biduuni khauf. al-qawaa'idu as-halu minash-shajaa'ah.
lines.id: Speaking without fear. Grammar is easier than courage.
lines.literal: that I-speak without fear. the-rules easier than the-courage.

lines.speaker: ضَيْف:
lines.text: كَلَامٌ صَحِيحٌ. وَمَاذَا سَتَفْعَلُ بَعْدَ الْعَوْدَةِ؟
lines.baca: kalaamun ṣahiih. wa maadhaa satafa'lu ba'dal-'audah?
lines.id: So true. And what will you do after you go home?
lines.literal: saying true. and what will-you-do after the-return?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: سَأُدَرِّسُ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ لِلْمُبْتَدِئِينَ، وَسَأَعُودُ إِلَيْكُمْ يَوْمًا مَا.
lines.baca: sa'udarrisul-'arabiyyata lil-mubtadi'iin, wa sa'a'uudu ilaikum yauman maa.
lines.id: I'll teach Arabic to beginners, and one day I'll come back here.
lines.literal: will-I-teach the-Arabic to-the-beginners, and will-I-return to-you(pl.) a-day some.

lines.speaker: ضَيْف:
lines.text: بِالتَّوْفِيقِ يَا صَدِيقِي. اَلْبَابُ مَفْتُوحٌ دَائِمًا.
lines.baca: bit-taufiiqi yaa ṣadiiqii. al-baabu maftuuhun daa'iman.
lines.id: Good luck, my friend. Our door is always open.
lines.literal: with-success O friend-my. the-door open always.

notes: **كُنْتُ + present verb = a past habit.** كُنْتُ أَقْرَأُ ("I used to read"), كُنْتَ تَعْمَلُ ("you used to work"). This structure describes something **ongoing** in the past, unlike قَرَأْتُ, which states a single finished event.
**قَبْلَ أَنْ + verb = "before ...".** قَبْلَ أَنْ تَأْتِيَ ("before you come"). Its partner is بَعْدَ أَنْ (after). Notice that أَنْ still triggers fathah on the verb ending, as in unit 16.

**أَصْبَحَ means "to become".** It works like كَانَ: the description takes fathah. أَصْبَحَتْ أَجْمَلَ سَنَةٍ ("it became the best year"). Its relatives: صَارَ (to become), مَا زَالَ (still), لَيْسَ (is not).

**أَجْمَلَ سَنَةٍ فِي حَيَاتِي — "-est" as an iḍafah.** You learned it in unit 12, and here it's used in the middle of a story, not as a grammar example. That's how everything you learn should end up.

**اَلْقَوَاعِدُ أَسْهَلُ مِنَ الشَّجَاعَةِ.** A sentence worth taking away from the whole book: grammar can be learned alone, the courage to speak can't. What separates people who end up speaking Arabic from those who stop at A1 is almost never intelligence.
**يَوْمًا مَا — "one day".** Tanwin fathah as an adverb again, plus مَا, which makes it vague. Similar forms: شَيْئًا مَا (something), مَكَانًا مَا (somewhere).

**لِلْمُبْتَدِئِينَ — the regular plural after a preposition.** مُبْتَدِئُونَ (beginners) becomes مُبْتَدِئِينَ because لِ comes before it. Same rule as صَدِيقَيْنِ and يَوْمَيْنِ in earlier units: the form changes as soon as it isn't the subject.

grammars.title: Linking sentences into a story
body: The difference between someone who "can make sentences" and someone who "can tell a story" isn't vocabulary but connectors. These eight words are enough for the whole of A1.
after: The exercise that improves your storytelling fastest: take five sentences you've already written and join them into two or three using the connectors above. The content doesn't grow at all, but the sound changes completely.

grammars.title: Three tenses in one story
after: These eight rows are the whole Arabic tense system you need at A1 — and you've already used all of them in the previous nineteen units. Only one thing is new in this unit: **switching between them within one story**, not one at a time in separate exercises.

sections.title: A framework for talking about yourself

blocks.text: A longer introduction in the Arab world almost always follows the same order. Memorize the framework and you'll never run out of things to say — or get stuck thinking of the next sentence.

blocks.title: Ten sentences that open every door
items: Memorize the ten sentences above, filled in with your own details, until they come out without thinking. That isn't cheating — it's exactly what any native speaker does when introducing themselves for the hundredth time.
Once those ten sentences flow, the conversation almost always carries on by itself: the other person will ask questions, and answering is much easier than starting.

blocks.text: لَا تَنْسَنَا is the warmest farewell in Arabic, and it rarely appears in textbooks. The reply: لَنْ أَنْسَاكُمْ أَبَدًا — "I will never forget you". These two sentences use لَا, لَنْ and أَبَدًا all at once, and now you know exactly why they take the forms they do.

exercises.prompt: Turn these into past habits with كَانَ.
Join into one sentence with the right connector.

exercises.prompt: Answer in complete sentences about yourself.
items: مَا أَصْعَبُ شَيْءٍ فِي هٰذِهِ اللُّغَةِ بِرَأْيِكَ؟
مَاذَا سَتَفْعَلُ بَعْدَ أَنْ تُنْهِيَ هٰذَا الْكِتَابَ؟

exercises.prompt: Write a complete story about yourself, at least twelve sentences, using the ten-part framework on the previous page. This is the book's final exercise — do it properly, then read it aloud and record yourself.

answers: كُنْتُ أَعْمَلُ فِي شَرِكَةٍ — كُنْتُ أَدْرُسُ فِي جَاكَرْتَا — كُنْتَ تَسْكُنُ فِي الْقَاهِرَةِ — كَانَ يَلْعَبُ كُرَةَ الْقَدَمِ — كُنَّا نَذْهَبُ إِلَى السُّوقِ

دَرَسْتُ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ لِأَنِّي أُحِبُّ اللُّغَاتِ. — أَكَلْتُ ثُمَّ نِمْتُ. — اَلدَّرْسُ صَعْبٌ لٰكِنَّهُ مُمْتِعٌ. — كُنْتُ مَشْغُولًا، لِذٰلِكَ لَمْ أَخْرُجْ. — فِي الْبِدَايَةِ كَانَ صَعْبًا، بَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ أَصْبَحَ سَهْلًا.

Example: كُنْتُ أَعْمَلُ مُهَنْدِسًا. — أَدْرُسُ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ لِأَنِّي أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَفْهَمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَالْأَخْبَارَ. — أَصْعَبُ شَيْءٍ هُوَ الْكَلَامُ بِدُونِ خَوْفٍ. — سَأَقْرَأُ قِصَصًا قَصِيرَةً وَسَأَبْحَثُ عَنْ مُدَرِّسٍ. — أَتَمَنَّى أَنْ أُسَافِرَ إِلَى مِصْرَ وَالْمَغْرِبِ.

Example: اِسْمِي بُودِي، أَنَا مِنْ جَاكَرْتَا وَعُمْرِي ثَلَاثُونَ سَنَةً — عِنْدِي أُخْتٌ وَاحِدَةٌ وَوَالِدَايَ يَسْكُنَانِ فِي بُوغُور — أَعْمَلُ مُهَنْدِسًا الْآنَ، وَقَبْلَ ذٰلِكَ كُنْتُ طَالِبًا — أَسْكُنُ فِي شَقَّةٍ صَغِيرَةٍ قُرْبَ الْعَمَلِ — أَسْتَيْقِظُ مُبَكِّرًا وَأَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ بِالْقِطَارِ — أُحِبُّ أَنْ أَقْرَأَ وَأَنْ أَمْشِيَ فِي الْمَسَاءِ — أَدْرُسُ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ لِأَنِّي كُنْتُ أَقْرَأُ الْحُرُوفَ وَلَا أَفْهَمُ — سَأُوَاصِلُ الدِّرَاسَةَ وَسَأُسَافِرُ إِلَى مِصْرَ يَوْمًا مَا، إِنْ شَاءَ اللهُ
wave: Record yourself reading the story from the last exercise. Keep the recording. In six months, record the same story again — and listen to both, one after the other.
